summary: The paper studies a simple rule for label noise: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit. On digits and breast cancer with symmetric noise at 20% and 40%, it reports about 71% pooled precision and high recall for flipped labels, and higher test accuracy than plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP. It reports a small cost on clean labels and states its scope openly (two small datasets, 5 seeds, one noise type).
strengths: The method is easy to state and to follow: one rule, three steps, K+1 fits. Section 3 describes it as a function with inputs and outputs before the details.
The teaser shows the pipeline (noisy labels, out-of-fold drop, refit) next to the result and the precision bar. A reader gets the idea without the text.

The text is candid about scope and limits. It says where the filter does not help (clean labels, the unstable breast cancer cell, 5x fit time) and that the mechanism is an argument, not a tested explanation.
Table 2 defines precision, recall, recovered share and the test in its caption. Fig. 2 plots paired gains with seed dots, so the spread is visible.
Related work ends each paragraph by saying how the filter differs, and it states plainly that the idea is Brodley and Friedl's single-algorithm filter.

weaknesses.issue: The headline claims are stronger than the results beneath them, and the paper contradicts itself on this. The abstract and intro say the filter beats LR 'in all but one paired noisy run' and 'in nearly every' run, and the intro says the evidence supports the claim 'in every noisy setting'. Yet breast cancer at 20% is not significant, breast cancer at 40% has sd of about 9 points, and only a fifth of the loss is recovered there. A reader cannot tell which cells the claim covers.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1 paragraph 4 and contributions; Sec. 4.2; Table 2
weaknesses.suggestion: State the same scoped claim in the abstract, the intro and the contribution bullets: the filter clearly helps on digits at both rates, helps on breast cancer at 40% but with high variance, and is not significant at 20%. Replace 'every noisy setting' with that sentence, and drop 'all but one run' unless the abstract also names which run.

weaknesses.issue: The opening claim of Sec. 4, 'finds most of the flipped labels', is carried by the pooled 71% precision, which mixes cells with different sizes and noise rates. The teaser presents 71% as one number. Recall is 79% in one cell and 98% in another, and a quarter to a third of the dropped samples are clean. The text says 'mostly' and 'most' without saying that precision at 20% on digits (64.6%) is only modestly above what the dropped fraction would suggest.
weaknesses.suggestion: Label the 71% in Fig. 1 as 'pooled over four noisy cells and 5 seeds'. Report the per-cell range of precision in the Sec. 4.1 text, and say what the pooled number weights. Add one sentence on what precision a random drop would give (the noise rate, 20% or 40%), so a reader sees how far above chance 65 to 76% is. The test against 50% does not show this.

weaknesses.issue: The comparison with the MLP is hard to read as a finding. The MLP is untuned, has no early stopping and no regularization, and it is the only nonlinear baseline. The paper's central story (a linear filter 'beats' the MLP by up to 28 points) rests on the weakest baseline, and the MLP is also not given the filtered data. The title and contribution bullet 2 lean on this win.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.3; Contribution 2; Fig. 2 orange bars; Sec. 5
weaknesses.suggestion: Say in the Fig. 2 caption and the Sec. 4.3 heading that the baseline is an untuned MLP. Reword the heading, e.g. 'An untuned MLP is hurt more by noisy labels than the filtered linear model'. Move the MLP win below the LR comparison in the contribution list. If the MLP trained on the filtered subset has been run, add it as one row in Table 1.

weaknesses.issue: Several terms and cell names change between places, which costs the reader effort. Table 1 uses 'none/low/high', Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 use 0/20/40, and Table 2 uses 20%/40%. The Fig. 1 dashed line 'clean-label accuracy of filter' is drawn once across two datasets. 'Recovered share' is defined only in the Table 2 caption but is used in the text. The panel 2 icon of the model looks like a neural network although the model is logistic regression.
weaknesses.where: Table 1 header; Fig. 1 panels 2 and 3; Table 2 caption; Sec. 4.2
weaknesses.suggestion: Use '0/20/40%' labels in all tables and figures. Draw the dashed line per dataset or drop it. Define 'recovered share' in one sentence in Sec. 4.2 or Sec. 3. Replace the network icon in Fig. 1 with a plain linear-classifier icon.

weaknesses.issue: The method section does not give what a reader needs to reproduce or judge the filter: how disagreement is computed for multiclass digits (argmax of the multiclass softmax?), whether the folds are drawn before or after the noise, the solver, and what 'standardized' fits on (each fold or all of the training set). The recovered-share formula divides by a quantity that is near zero when noise costs little, which makes the cell comparison unstable.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 3 Procedure; Sec. 3 Setup; Table 2 caption
weaknesses.suggestion: Add two lines to Sec. 3 on argmax disagreement, and on whether scaling is fit inside each fold. Give 'recovered' for each cell with the raw accuracy loss it divides by, or drop the column.

weaknesses.issue: The text is hard to follow in places because of repetition and misplaced material. Sec. 4 opens with a sentence that repeats the subsection headings. The clean-label paragraph has a one-sentence orphan for breast cancer. The sentence about recomputing numbers 'with the Scriptorium pipeline' sits in the method section and is not part of the method. The contribution 'An honest account of cost and scope' describes a virtue instead of a result. Section 5 repeats the limitations and the contributions almost line by line.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 3 last paragraph; Sec. 4 opening and clean-label subsection; Sec. 1 bullet 3; Sec. 5
weaknesses.suggestion: Cut the pipeline sentence from Sec. 3 or move it to the acknowledgments. Merge the two breast cancer sentences into the clean-label paragraph. Rewrite bullet 3 as 'We measure the clean-label cost, the fit time and the failure cell'. Shorten Sec. 5 to the take-away and the limits not already stated in Sec. 2 and 4.

weaknesses.issue: Length and layout: the paper has two full-width tables, two figures and a dense Sec. 4 in a 4-page limit. Table 1 is shrunk with resizebox, which risks tiny type. Sec. 4 depends on three artifacts (Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 2), and Fig. 2 and Table 1 show largely the same differences.
weaknesses.suggestion: Check the compiled page count with references excluded and check Table 1 type size. If space is short, drop Fig. 2 and put the paired differences with CIs as one row block in Table 1, or keep Fig. 2 and drop the corresponding text numbers.

questions: Is the 71% precision in Fig. 1 pooled by samples or by runs, and how does it compare with a random drop at the same rate?
Which noisy run does the abstract's 'all but one' refer to, and is it breast cancer at 20%?
How does disagreement work for the 10-class digits problem: is it the argmax of the softmax, and does the folding respect the noise draw?
Does an MLP trained on the filtered subset close the gap on clean data, or is the clean-data tie a property of the model?
